amendments.rule: An English function word the ASV supplies for an adverbial accusative belongs to the noun whose case-function licenses it — *as a bird*, *to your mountain* — and is never `added`. **An appositional or measure nominal the ASV introduces with a supplied preposition is read the same way.** Where a noun or numeral stands in the clause with no preposition and no object marker on it, and the ASV writes an *of* or a *for* before it to state what that nominal contributes, the word is that nominal's own rendering: `אֹרֶךְ חֲמִשָּׁה וְעֶשְׂרִים אֶלֶף` → *the length ... of five and twenty thousand*, `תֹּכֶן אֶחָד` → *of one measure*, `לַאֲחֻזָּה עֶשְׂרִים לְשָׁכֹת` → *for a possession ..., for twenty chambers*, `חַטָּאת שְׂעִיר עִזִּים` → *a he goat ... for a sin offering*. It goes to the word it stands before, which is the noun or numeral opening that phrase, and the unit still heads on the word carrying the lexeme under rules 24 and 31; the supplied preposition is never the head. **Read *an *of* or a *for** as any preposition the ASV writes for the nominal's own contribution, and not as a closed list.** What licenses the word is that a bare nominal stands in the clause and the English needs a word to say what it contributes there, so read the condition and not the lemma, exactly as rule 40 does for the preposition it silences: a comparative *as* before a nominal the ASV construes as a comparison — `פַּלְגֵי מַיִם` → ***as*** *the watercourses* — an agent *by* before a bare nominal the ASV construes with a passive participle — `מְבַקְשֵׁי מָוֶת` → *driven to and fro* ***by*** *them that seek death* — and a *with* or an *in* before a nominal standing in a `מִן` comparison — `אֵשֶׁת מִדְיָנִים` → ***with*** *a contentious woman*, `בֵּית חָבֶר` → ***in*** *a wide house* — all go to the nominal on the same terms as an *of* or a *for*, and this rule's first sentence already writes *as* and *to* for the adverbial accusative. Three limits, each stated where it belongs. A word an object marker stands to take is the marker's under rule 16, and an *as for* the ASV writes before a topicalized phrase no marker and no preposition stands on is `added` under that rule rather than this one, since a nominal's fronting is not a case-function. A preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own bare object is the verb's under rule 44, and this rule's own closing paragraph disposes of one a predicate's valency needs. And a coordinating or subordinating connective the ASV writes beside such a phrase is not a word spent on the nominal at all: rules 14 and 55 count those against the morphemes that could carry them. **A preposition standing elsewhere in the clause that has already taken an English word of its own does not make such a word a surplus.** Rule 52's count governs two English words offered to one morpheme, and here each phrase has a rendering of its own, so a written `לְ` rendered *for a possession* does not silence the *for* the ASV writes before the phrase standing beside it. **But the noun must be present.** Where the ASV supplies the head noun as well as the function word, no morpheme is there to carry either, and the whole supplied phrase is its own `added` unit under rule 30: `חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת בַּחֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת` → *five hundred* ***in length*** *by five hundred* ***in breadth*** supplies both the preposition and the dimension noun in a clause whose Hebrew names neither, exactly as the italic ***reeds*** of `חֲמִשָּׁה וְעֶשְׂרִים אֶלֶף` supplies a measure noun. Test by subtraction as rules 16 and 31 do: drop the English and ask whether a Hebrew noun standing in the clause has lost the relation it bears, or whether what has gone is a noun the Hebrew never wrote. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it either way and decides nothing, by rule 7. **And a bare noun that completes a predicate's own valency is not an adverbial accusative at all.** Where a verb or a predicate adjective governs a bare noun as its complement — no preposition and no object marker on it — and the English predicate can reach that complement only through a preposition the ASV has written, that word answers to the predicate's valency and joins the predicate's unit under rule 44, while the noun keeps its own English: `מָלֵאתָ` → *thou art full* ***of*** *the judgment* and `מָלֵא דָשֶׁן` → *would be full* ***of*** *fatness* both give the *of* to `מָלֵא`, headed on *full*, and leave `דִין` and `דֶשֶׁן` their own words. Decide it by asking whether the ASV had a relation to choose: where the English predicate admits no other word before such a complement — *full of* is the only way English writes it — the preposition is the predicate's, and where the word states what the noun contributes to the clause and another would have served, this rule governs and the word is the noun's, as it does for `יָזֹקּוּ מָטָר` → *distil* ***in*** *rain* and `כַּבִּיר כֹּחַ` → *mighty* ***in*** *strength*. Read the English predicate rather than where the noun stands, since Hebrew writes such a complement before its predicate as readily as after it, and JOB.36.16 and JOB.36.17 are the two shapes in one chapter.
amendments.why: Rule 33's appositional-and-measure sentence names *of* and *for* and nothing else, and PRO.21 fell outside that list four times with the same construction underneath: a bare written nominal and a preposition the ASV supplies to state what it contributes (*as* 21.1, *by* 21.6, *with* and *in* 21.9 and 21.19). The rule's own first sentence already writes *as a bird* and *to your mountain* for the adverbial accusative, so the narrow list was an accident of which examples the measure chapters supplied, not a distinction the rule was drawing; nothing in the corpus tables returned here treats a supplied preposition before a bare nominal any other way. The amendment widens the list where it stands rather than adding a rule that points back at it, and it names the three exclusions — rule 16's *as for*, rule 44's valency preposition, rules 14 and 55's connectives — so the widening cannot be read as a licence to hand any stray English word to the nearest noun. It changes no existing outcome: every example already in the rule is placed exactly as before.

conventions: A preposition the ASV supplies before a bare written nominal joins that nominal's unit under rule 33 and is never `added`, whatever preposition it is: the comparative *as* of 21.1 פַּלְגֵי מַיִם → *as the watercourses*, the agent *by* of 21.6 מְבַקְשֵׁי מָוֶת → *by them that seek death*, and the *with* and *in* of 21.9 and 21.19 before the members of a מִן comparison. The boundary the chapter drew the other way twice is rule 16's: an *as for* before a topicalized phrase carrying no object marker and no preposition is `added` (21.8, 21.29), a fronting being no case-function. Read whether a Hebrew nominal stands under the supplied word, not which English preposition it is.

Where a construct chain is rendered attributively under rule 28, a determiner the ASV supplies joins the morpheme its English head noun renders, whichever side of the chain that is, and the unit is discontinuous around the attributive. The construct carries it in אִישׁ מַחְסוֹר → *a poor man* (21.17), אֵשֶׁת מִדְיָנִים → *a contentious woman* (21.9, 21.19), עֵד־כְּזָבִים → *A false witness* (21.28) and לְשׁוֹן שָׁקֶר → *a lying tongue* (21.6); the rectum carries it in רוּם עֵינַיִם → *A high look* (21.4), where the ASV's head noun is *look* and the construct supplies the attributive. This is rule 15's *the noun of the expression, not its leftmost word* read for a chain rather than for a numeral.

report: Cross-verse consistency: no split found. Every candidate bucket that showed two treatments is ASV-driven. The waw of 21.5 has a written *But* and the waw of 21.9 no connective at all; the לְ of 21.31 has a written *against* while the לְ of 21.12 stands before a bare direct object (rule 40); the מִן of 21.3 has a written *more* and those of 21.9/21.19 a bare *Than*; the assimilated article of 21.14 has a written *the* in the second colon and none in the first. A difference the source licenses is not a split.

Because the lemma table is blind to `added` units, I audited the supplied English separately, verse by verse. The chapter draws two boundaries, each of them twice, and draws them the same way both times. A preposition supplied before a bare written nominal joins that nominal under rule 33 — *as* (21.1), *by* (21.6), *with* and *in* (21.9), *with* (21.19) — while an *as for* before a topicalized phrase carrying no marker is `added` under rule 16 (21.8, 21.29). A supplied lexical verb is `added` (21.5 *tend* and *hasteth*, 21.18 *cometh*) and a supplied copula never is. A supplied determiner joins the nominal it determines in all 25 verses that carry one, and is nowhere `added`.

The three presentative frames go to three different licensing morphemes — the prepositional predicate in 21.20 (rules 49 and 20), the finite verb in 21.26 (rule 17), the existential אַיִן in 21.30 (rule 50) — while the three impersonal *It*s of 21.9, 21.15 and 21.19 are `added`. That is rule 20's own distinction applied consistently, not two analyses of one construction.

Rule 49's copula on a prepositional predicate is applied alike in 21.1, 21.20 and 21.31, and 21.31 rightly declines rule 49's fused-genitive case because the ASV writes an *of* for the preposition. I re-read 21.1 against rule 49's closing paragraph, which sends a copula standing beside an adjunct to the nominal predicate instead. The verse's reading holds — the supplied *as* the ASV writes before *the watercourses* is its own declaration that it construes פַּלְגֵי־מַיִם as an adverbial comparison and בְּיַד־יְהוָה as the predicate — but the competing reading is material and was not named. The one patch below adds it. No edge, head or status changes anywhere in the chapter.

BSB: all five disagreements are the documented convention difference and none is an error. 21.9 וּ, 21.11 לְ, 21.12 לְ and 21.29 בְּ are morphemes the ASV's recasting leaves with no English word at all (rules 14 and 40), and 21.31 הַ stands on a noun the ASV writes bare (rule 29). BSB attaches each to its phrase; that is its convention, not a correction of ours.

The validator's 39 repeated review notes are almost all restatements of contract rules that already bind every verse (`Preposition.`, `Construct noun with supplied *the* (rule 29)`). Two of them are chapter-wide judgments a later reader would have to rediscover, and those two are logged below; the rest are deliberately not.
